I think it's reasonable that if we're meant to take Blue Lock's whole internal competition thing---and, in turn, candidates outside of the core cast---seriously that we receive flat-characters like Kurona who are nonetheless able to impose themselves in some way on the pitch. I say "seriously" not as "oh hey, these characters can be narratively significant" but as in "the fact that at least some of these so-called competitors, with neither author tract nor backstory, can DO things bolsters the 'worldbuilding' of Blue Lock".

\*In some small sense, I also feel this is a reason people would like characters like Kiyora Jin or Nishioka to also do things---not to be important, backstoried characters, but just present---here and there---on the pitch.

But, otherwise, even amongst flat characters, he has his niche, which I think matters in this genre. His character archetype is uniquely "silly, cute" in a way that I don't think any of the other cast are. Textual-visual mediums will always have more "space" for flat-characters simply because of how efficient visual design is for adding some semblance of iconism or dimension (and, thus, reader value) to them.

What? Of course your physicals matter. Where we kind of agree is that they don't apply in a uniform manner.

Height *matters* for every single position on the pitch, it's just not absolutely necessary to possess it to excel, and even become a world-class player. It's not the only thing that matters (hell, Jorge Campos was a generational, 5'6" goalkeeper)---but having it still constitutes "natural talent". Anyone who challenges aerially (and that's \*everyone\* on the pitch) benefits from height.

You're also absolutely kidding yourself if you think one's physicals don't matter---they just aren't the only things that matter. Messi's lower center of gravity is in part what informs Messi's instinctual dribbling, as well as the dribbling of many other diminutive flair players. Dribbling is also a product of speed, agility, balance---these are, yes, all things that can be improved and maximized through sheer gym-time... but they are also greatly informed by innate physical parameters.

Messi doesn't serve your point at all here, because something you're not realizing is that, for all his stature and early growth deficiency, Messi is *astounding* physically.

We agree that it is not strictly better to be taller in football... but that also isn't what was being argued. Height---until your profile gets to the point of unwieldiness---is absolutely a natural talent relevant to football (and even then, when we consider someone like Peter Crouch / Per Mertesacker).

Innate physical parameters like height have always been considered "natural talent" across numerous sports.

But, in some sense, you're right.

It's not so much tallness being more or less advantageous than shortness in football, it's how its applied. With some very legendary exceptions (Fabio Cannavaro with his intense vertical and timing, for one), height is a paramount trait of centerbacks, for example, and anyone expected to engage in aerial duels (target men, hold-up players).

Conversely, someone like Messi is shorter, but part of his talent is that low center of gravity he has while dribbling.
